problems.stem: A teacher says, "Our district AI policy never mentions chatbots for grading, so I am free to upload student essays to one." What is the interpretation error?
options: No error; if the policy is silent, anything is allowed.
Silence is not permission; FERPA and the district's data-sharing rules still govern uploading identifiable student work to a third-party tool.
The teacher should upload the essays faster.
The policy must list every tool by name to apply.
problems.explanation: A gap in the written policy does not authorize the practice. Governing privacy law and broader data rules still apply, and clarification should be sought.

problems.stem: A policy states "AI tools may not be used to complete student assessments." A teacher reads this to mean she cannot use an AI tool to generate accessibility supports, like read-aloud, for a student with an IEP during a test. What is the better interpretation?
options: Her literal reading is correct; ban all AI on assessments.
Read for purpose: the rule targets students offloading the thinking, not removing a documented accessibility accommodation, which the IEP requires.
Ignore the IEP because the AI policy is newer.
The two rules cancel out, so do nothing.
problems.explanation: Interpreting toward the policy's intent, integrity of the assessment, preserves a required accommodation that a literal reading would wrongly block.

problems.stem: Before letting students use an AI tutoring app, which set of rules must a teacher check together?
options: The AI-use memo plus FERPA, the app's terms of service and minimum age, parental-consent rules, and any IEP/504 obligations.
Only whether other teachers use it.
problems.explanation: AI decisions sit at the intersection of several policies. One memo rarely answers privacy, consent, age, and special-education questions on its own.

problems.stem: A two-year-old acceptable-use policy requires an AI plagiarism detector that you have documented falsely flags multilingual students. You must apply policy this week. What is the most defensible action?
options: Apply the detector as written and accept the false flags, since policy is final.
Follow the policy minimally while documenting the false-positive cases and formally routing the evidence to the policy owner to request revision.
Quietly ignore the policy and tell no one.
problems.explanation: Policies are not static. A teacher applies the current rule while documenting demonstrated harm and routing it to decision-makers so the policy can be revised.

problems.stem: Provide a concise response that demonstrates this learning objective: Document a bounded AI/software support move with accepted and rejected suggestions.
problems.expected_answer: The response accurately demonstrates the section objective: Document a bounded AI/software support move with accepted and rejected suggestions, using relevant section concepts, evidence, or calculations.
problems.explanation: This direct-evidence item is used when no closed-response item adequately samples the objective. Score it with the section concepts and worked examples as the rubric.
